blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Say you inherit a dataset and your instinct is to jump straight to training a model. That instinct is understandable, the model is the fun part, but it is also how people burn a week fitting a regression on an income column that is so heavily skewed the coefficients barely mean anything, or building a classifier on a target that is 95 percent one class without noticing. The fix for both problems already existed in the data before you ever wrote a line of modeling code. You just had not looked yet.

The statistical-operations lesson already gave you the individual tools: mean, median, standard deviation, percentiles, the axis parameter, all of it. This lesson does not add new formulas to that toolkit. It shows you how to point those tools at a whole realistic DataFrame, in a specific order, every single time you meet a new dataset, before you touch a model. That deliberate order is what people mean when they say exploratory data analysis, or EDA for short.

Running this routine is cheap. A few minutes of describe, skew, kurtosis, and a couple of categorical checks will tell you exactly which columns need a log transform, which ones are hiding outlier prone tails, and whether your categories are balanced enough to trust. Skip it, and you find all of that out later, the hard way, when your model quietly underperforms and you have no idea why.

blocks.alt: Skipping the statistics routine leading to hidden problems surfacing late, versus running it first leading to a model built on understood data
blocks.caption: The five minutes this routine takes is cheaper than debugging a model later.

items: df.describe as the deliberate starting point of the routine, not a one-off inspection command.
df.skew to measure how lopsided a numeric column is, and which direction it leans.
df.kurt to measure how heavy or light a column's tails are compared to normal.
value_counts with normalize true to read proportions in a categorical column instead of raw counts.
pd.crosstab to see how two categorical columns relate to each other.
A worked example running the whole routine end to end on one realistic dataset.

blocks.title: No new statistics here
blocks.content: Every individual statistic in this lesson, mean, std, quartiles, was already covered in statistical-operations. What is new is the routine itself, the habit of running them together, in order, on a whole DataFrame, as the very first thing you do with new data.

blocks.text: 2. describe Revisited as the Starting Point of a Routine

The data-inspection lesson introduced df.describe() as one tool among several, sitting next to head, shape, info, and dtypes, useful for getting a first feel of a new DataFrame. That was true, but it undersold describe a little. Here is the reframe: describe is not just one inspection command out of many, it is the correct first move in a repeatable, structured routine that you run on every dataset before modeling.

Everything you need to read that table was already covered in statistical-operations and data-inspection: count catches missing values, mean and std describe center and spread, the quartiles sketch the shape. What matters now is what you do with that reading. Notice that annual_income has a mean of 58,400 but a max of 410,000, and a 75th percentile of only 68,000. That gap between the 75th percentile and the max is your first hint of a long right tail, and the next two sections turn that hint into an actual number.

blocks.alt: A chain from describe to skew to kurt to value counts to crosstab representing one continuous routine
blocks.caption: describe is step one of a routine, not a report you glance at once and forget.

blocks.title: Read describe for shape, not just for values
blocks.content: Do not just skim describe for outright errors like a negative age. Compare mean to median, that is the 50% row, and compare the 75th percentile to the max. Big gaps in either comparison are exactly what the next two sections quantify directly.

blocks.text: 2.1 From a One-Off Check to a Repeatable Routine
Treat the following as a checklist you run on any new DataFrame, in this order, before you write a single line of modeling code. Each step below gets its own section in this lesson.

items: Run describe on the numeric columns to see center, spread, and quartiles.
Run skew on the numeric columns to quantify asymmetry.
Run kurt on the numeric columns to quantify tail weight.
Run value_counts with normalize true on every categorical column to check balance.
Run crosstab between pairs of categorical columns that plausibly relate to each other.
Move on to correlation analysis, the next lesson, for numeric to numeric relationships.

blocks.text: 3. Measuring Skewness with df.skew()

describe hints at asymmetry through the gap between mean, median, and the tails, but a hint is not a number you can act on. df.skew() turns that hint into a single value per column that tells you exactly how lopsided the distribution is, and which direction it leans.

code.content:
df[['age', 'annual_income', 'monthly_spend', 'num_purchases']].skew()

# age               0.42
# annual_income     1.92
# monthly_spend     2.31
# num_purchases     1.15
# dtype: float64

blocks.text: A skew of 0 means a perfectly symmetric distribution. A positive skew means the tail stretches toward higher values. A negative skew means the tail stretches toward lower values. The sign tells you the direction, the size tells you how severe it is, and both matter for what you do next.
3.1 Positive Skew: A Long Tail Stretching Toward Higher Values

annual_income above has a skew of 1.92, clearly positive. Picture why: most customers earn somewhere ordinary, a smaller group earns noticeably more, and a tiny handful earn a lot more than everyone else. That small group of very high earners drags the mean up above the median while barely moving the median at all, because the median only cares about the middle position, not the magnitude of the extremes.

blocks.alt: A distribution where most values cluster low, a few sit very high, and the tail stretches to the right pulling the mean above the median
blocks.caption: Positive skew, the classic shape for income, prices, and transaction amounts.

blocks.title: A useful gut check
blocks.content: If the mean sits noticeably above the median in describe output, expect a positive skew value. If the mean sits below the median, expect negative skew. skew just confirms and quantifies what that comparison already suggested.

blocks.text: 3.2 Negative Skew: A Long Tail Stretching Toward Lower Values

Negative skew is the mirror image. Picture an exam where most students score close to full marks and only a handful score poorly. The bulk of the distribution sits high, a thin tail stretches down toward low scores, and the mean gets pulled below the median by that small group of low scorers.

blocks.alt: A distribution where most values cluster high, a few sit very low, and the tail stretches to the left pulling the mean below the median
blocks.caption: Negative skew, common in capped scores, ratings, and near ceiling measurements.

blocks.text: Neither direction is inherently good or bad. Skew is just a description of shape. What you do about it depends on how large the value is and what you plan to do with the column next.
3.3 How Much Skew Is Worth Addressing
There is no universal legal threshold here, but the following rule of thumb is widely used in practice and is a reasonable default to reach for.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Absolute skew value","Interpretation"],"rows":[["Below 0.5","Roughly symmetric. Usually fine to leave alone."],["0.5 to 1.0","Moderate skew. Worth a look, not always worth transforming."],["Above 1.0","Substantial skew. Generally worth transforming before modeling with methods sensitive to it."]]}

blocks.text: By that rule, num_purchases at 1.15 and annual_income at 1.92 both cross into substantial territory, while age at 0.42 is close enough to symmetric to leave untouched. Treat this as a starting point for judgment, not a strict cutoff. A skew of 0.95 on a column that a tree based model will consume is a very different situation from the same skew feeding into linear regression.
3.4 Where the Fix Actually Lives

This lesson's job stops at detection. Once skew crosses a threshold you care about, the actual fix, applying a log transform for strong positive skew or a gentler square root transform for milder cases, is covered in full in the feature-transformation lesson, including exactly when to reach for log versus log1p and how to reverse the transform later. Think of this section as the smoke detector and that lesson as the fire extinguisher.

blocks.alt: A skew value flagged above threshold in this lesson feeding forward into a log or sqrt fix applied in the feature transformation lesson
blocks.caption: Detection happens here. The fix itself lives one lesson ahead.

blocks.text: 4. Measuring Kurtosis with df.kurt()

Skew tells you which way a distribution leans. df.kurt() answers a different question entirely: how heavy or light are the tails compared to a normal distribution. A column can have almost zero skew, perfectly symmetric, and still have tails that are far more extreme than a bell curve would predict.

code.content:
df[['age', 'annual_income', 'monthly_spend', 'num_purchases']].kurt()

# age              -0.18
# annual_income     5.40
# monthly_spend     8.70
# num_purchases     2.60
# dtype: float64

blocks.text: pandas reports excess kurtosis, meaning a normal distribution scores 0 here, not 3. A value near 0 means tails behave about like a normal distribution. A positive value means heavier tails, more extreme values sitting further out than normal would predict. A negative value means lighter, flatter tails with fewer extreme values than normal.
4.1 High Kurtosis Means Outlier Prone Tails

monthly_spend above scores 8.70, a genuinely high kurtosis. That number is telling you, before you have looked at a single individual row, that this column is likely to contain values sitting unusually far from the bulk of the data. This is exactly the situation the outlier-detection lesson is built for: once kurtosis has flagged a column as tail heavy, running the IQR rule or a z-score check on that specific column is how you find and evaluate the actual candidate rows.

blocks.alt: A normal distribution baseline compared to a high kurtosis column with heavier outlier prone tails, feeding into an IQR or z-score check
blocks.caption: High kurtosis is the shape level warning. IQR and z-score are how you act on it row by row.

blocks.title: Kurtosis has the same circularity problem as z-score
blocks.content: A single wildly extreme value can inflate kurtosis on its own, the same way one extreme value distorts a mean or a z-score, as covered in outlier-detection. Treat a high kurtosis reading as a reason to look closer, not as final proof of anything.

blocks.text: 5. Categorical Distributions with value_counts(normalize=True)

Every statistic so far in this lesson, and in statistical-operations before it, describes a numeric column. Real DataFrames also carry categorical columns, region, subscription tier, device type, and describe by default skips right past them. You need a different, equally quick habit for those columns, and value_counts is it.

code.content:
df['subscription_tier'].value_counts()

# Free       3405
# Basic      1195
# Premium     400
# Name: subscription_tier, dtype: int64

df['subscription_tier'].value_counts(normalize=True)

# Free       0.681
# Basic      0.239
# Premium    0.080
# Name: subscription_tier, dtype: float64

blocks.text: The raw counts are correct but they are hard to reason about on their own, especially once you start comparing datasets of different sizes or subsets of the same dataset. Passing normalize=True converts every count into a proportion of the whole column, so the numbers always sum to 1 regardless of how many rows you have. That single argument turns value_counts from a tally into an actual distribution you can reason about at a glance.

blocks.alt: Raw counts converted by normalize true into proportions of the whole, revealing class balance directly
blocks.caption: Proportions are comparable across datasets of any size. Raw counts are not.

blocks.title: A genuinely practical habit
blocks.content: Run value_counts with normalize true on your target column before you train a classifier. A split like 68 percent, 24 percent, 8 percent tells you immediately that plain accuracy will be a misleading metric and that you likely need stratified sampling or class weighting.

blocks.text: 5.1 Reading Class Balance and Category Dominance

The subscription_tier proportions above show Free at 68 percent, Basic at 24 percent, and Premium at only 8 percent. That is a meaningfully imbalanced categorical column. If you were building a model to predict who upgrades to Premium, a naive model that always guesses Free would already be right 68 percent of the time, which tells you accuracy alone will not be a useful metric later, and that this imbalance is worth carrying forward as a modeling decision, not just a curiosity you noticed once.
6. Cross Tabulation with pd.crosstab()

value_counts tells you about one categorical column in isolation. Plenty of real questions involve two categorical columns at once: does region relate to subscription tier at all, or are they independent of each other? pd.crosstab() answers exactly that, by building a joint frequency table between two columns.

code.content:
pd.crosstab(df['region'], df['subscription_tier'])

# subscription_tier  Free  Basic  Premium
# region
# East                875    275      100
# North               825    310      115
# South                730    210       60
# West                975    440      225

blocks.alt: A region column and a tier column both feeding into pd.crosstab producing a joint frequency table that reveals the relationship between the two
blocks.caption: crosstab is value_counts for two categorical columns at the same time.

blocks.text: Each cell counts how many rows share that particular combination of region and tier. Reading raw counts across regions of different total size is awkward though, exactly the same problem raw value_counts had, and normalize solves it the same way here too.

blocks.title: crosstab defaults to raw counts
blocks.content: Just like value_counts, plain crosstab hands you raw counts. Reach for the normalize argument, covered next, whenever you actually want to compare proportions across rows or columns of different sizes.

blocks.text: 6.1 Normalizing a Crosstab for Percentages
Passing normalize='index' converts every row into percentages of that row's own total, which is the natural way to ask a question like, within each region, what share of customers picked each tier.

code.content:
pd.crosstab(df['region'], df['subscription_tier'], normalize='index')

# subscription_tier  Free  Basic  Premium
# region
# East               0.70  0.22   0.08
# North              0.66  0.25   0.09
# South              0.73  0.21   0.06
# West               0.58  0.28   0.14

blocks.text: Now the comparison is fair regardless of how many customers each region has. West stands out immediately, at 0.14 its Premium share is close to double every other region's. That is precisely the kind of relationship raw counts would have buried under West simply having more total customers.
7. What Comes Next: Correlation for Numeric Relationships

This lesson closed the loop on two things: the shape of individual numeric columns, through describe, skew, and kurt, and the relationship between categorical columns, through value_counts and crosstab. One relationship is still missing. How does annual_income relate to monthly_spend? Does num_purchases move together with income, or not at all? That is a numeric to numeric question, and crosstab does not answer it, correlation does. That is exactly what the next lesson, correlation-analysis, covers.

blocks.alt: Categorical to categorical relationships covered here, and numeric to numeric relationships covered next in the correlation analysis lesson
blocks.caption: One relationship type down, one to go, right in the next lesson.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: A Full EDA Routine on a Realistic Dataset

Time to run the entire routine end to end on one dataset, the same way you would on day one with any new project. The dataset is a simplified customer table from a fictional online store called TechCart: 5000 rows, with age, annual_income, monthly_spend, and num_purchases as numeric columns, and region and subscription_tier as categorical columns.

blocks.alt: The customer dataset flowing through describe, skew, kurt, value counts, and crosstab as one continuous end to end routine
blocks.caption: The same five steps from this lesson, run back to back on one real table.

blocks.text: 8.1 Step One: describe

Already a few things stand out. annual_income has a mean of 58,400 well below its max of 410,000, with the 75th percentile at only 68,000, a huge gap. monthly_spend shows the same pattern even more sharply, a max of 940 against a 75th percentile of 112. age looks tame by comparison, mean and median close together. Those are hints. The next two steps turn them into numbers.
8.2 Step Two: skew

code.content:
df[['age', 'annual_income', 'monthly_spend', 'num_purchases']].skew()

# age               0.42
# annual_income     1.92
# monthly_spend     2.31
# num_purchases     1.15
# dtype: float64

blocks.text: The hint from describe checks out. annual_income and monthly_spend both cross well past the 1.0 threshold from earlier in this lesson, confirming strong positive skew. num_purchases sits just above 1.0 too, moderate but still worth noting. age at 0.42 stays comfortably in symmetric territory, matching how close its mean and median already looked in describe.
8.3 Step Three: kurt

code.content:
df[['age', 'annual_income', 'monthly_spend', 'num_purchases']].kurt()

# age              -0.18
# annual_income     5.40
# monthly_spend     8.70
# num_purchases     2.60
# dtype: float64

blocks.text: monthly_spend's kurtosis of 8.70 is the loudest signal in the whole table. Combined with its skew of 2.31, this column is both heavily lopsided and carrying unusually extreme values in its tail. annual_income is right behind it at 5.40. age, again, looks the most ordinary, its slightly negative kurtosis just means marginally flatter tails than a normal distribution, nothing alarming.
8.4 Step Four: value_counts

code.content:
df['subscription_tier'].value_counts(normalize=True)

# Free       0.681
# Basic      0.239
# Premium    0.080
# Name: subscription_tier, dtype: float64

blocks.text: The target-like column here, subscription_tier, is meaningfully imbalanced. Nearly seven in ten customers sit on the Free tier, and Premium customers make up less than one in ten. Worth remembering for whenever this dataset feeds a classification model down the line.
8.5 Step Five: crosstab

code.content:
pd.crosstab(df['region'], df['subscription_tier'], normalize='index')

# subscription_tier  Free  Basic  Premium
# region
# East               0.70  0.22   0.08
# North              0.66  0.25   0.09
# South              0.73  0.21   0.06
# West               0.58  0.28   0.14

blocks.text: The imbalance from step four is not uniform across regions. West has a noticeably higher Premium share, 0.14 versus roughly 0.06 to 0.09 everywhere else. That is a real relationship between region and tier, exactly the kind of pattern crosstab exists to surface, and it is the sort of thing a model, or a marketing team, would want to know about directly.
8.6 What This Routine Tells You to Do Next
Five quick steps, and the dataset has already told you most of what you need to plan the rest of this module's workflow before touching a model.

blocks.alt: Findings from the routine, high income skew, high spend kurtosis, and tier imbalance, each feeding into a specific concrete preprocessing decision
blocks.caption: Every finding from this routine points at a specific, actionable next step.

blocks.title: This is the whole point of the lesson
blocks.content: None of these five steps took more than a couple of lines of code, and together they already told you which columns need transforming, which need outlier checks, and how to split your data responsibly. That is the entire value of running statistics as a routine instead of skipping straight to modeling.

blocks.text: 9. Summary and What Comes Next

items: describe is the deliberate first step of an EDA routine, not a one-off command, use the gap between mean, median, and the tails as your first hint of trouble.
skew quantifies asymmetry: positive skew stretches toward higher values, negative skew stretches toward lower values, and roughly above 1.0 in absolute value is generally worth addressing.
The actual fix for high skew, log or square root transforms, lives in the feature-transformation lesson. This lesson only detects it.
kurt measures tail weight relative to normal. High kurtosis flags a column likely to contain the kind of extreme values the outlier-detection lesson's IQR and z-score methods are built to catch.
value_counts with normalize true turns raw category counts into comparable proportions, the fastest way to spot class imbalance or category dominance.
crosstab extends that same idea to two categorical columns at once, revealing relationships that raw per-column counts would hide.
Numeric to numeric relationships are the one piece this lesson deliberately left out. That is exactly where correlation-analysis, the next lesson, picks up.

blocks.text: You now have a full, repeatable routine: describe, skew, kurt, value_counts, crosstab, run in that order on any new dataset before you touch a model. Every finding it produces is either a green light to move forward or a specific, named task, a transform, an outlier check, a stratified split, that some other lesson in this module already knows how to handle.
